list.listitem: Suspect envenomation after any marine injury. C
Treat all vertebrate fish envenomations with hot water bath and analgesics. Consider presence of foreign bodies. B
Treat sea urchin envenomations with hot water immersion, analgesics, and foreign body removal. C

Many jellyfish stings respond to hot water immersion. Virtually all invertebrate envenomations can be treated with topical acetic acid solution, decontamination by scraping, copious flushing, analgesics, and antipruritics. Avoid rubbing the area, or applying fresh water or liquor. B
Where deadly species are native, administer specific antivenom early for signs of systemic envenomations. C

background.definition: Envenomation occurs when a toxin is injected by a venom delivery system such as a bite or sting. Hundreds of marine species are capable of causing significant envenomations in swimmers and divers. A few species cause serious, sometimes fatal, envenomations.

list.listitem: The true incidence is unknown. Estimates of cases per year range up to 100,000.
Jellyfish and man-of-war infestations are common causes of beach closure and can adversely impact tourism-driven economies.
Coelenterates, particularly the Cnidaria (jellyfish, Portuguese man-of-war, anemones, etc.) cause the vast majority of marine envenomations.

Many vertebrate fishes also cause envenomations after accidental contact (e.g., stingrays trod upon by victims walking in the surf) or while being handled by hobbyists, divers, or fishermen (e.g., lionfish).
Sea urchins are a common cause of envenomations to divers and snorklers.
Animals with potentially lethal venom include the Australian box jellyfish, sea snakes, cone snail, blue-ringed octopus, and stonefish.
Cnidaria (jellyfish, man-of-war, etc.) envenomate when tiny stinging cells (nematocysts) penetrate human skin and inject a complex venom.
Vertebrate fishes (stingrays, lionfish, etc.) envenomate through a stinger or multiple spines.
Sea urchins envenomate through spines that can penetrate gloves and footwear, sometimes breaking off into the wound.
Sea snakes envenomate through small, fragile fangs. Such envenomations are rare.
Anaphylaxis and anaphylactoid reactions may also occur after any envenomation.

Swimmers and divers should have a familiarity with dangerous creatures in the area and wear appropriate protective clothing (such as wet suits). Inappropriate handling is a well-recognized cause of envenomation. C
Commercially available topical preparations to inhibit jellyfish stings have been advocated, but efficacy has not been well established. B
Suspect envenomation after any marine injury. C
Linear lesions or wheals with immediate pain and pruritus suggest invertebrate (e.g., jellyfish, man-of-war) envenomations. B
Painful puncture wounds suggest vertebrate envenomations. C

Jellyfish and man-of-war envenomations cause wheals or linear, erythematous lesions with intense burning and pruritis. Victims may not see the creature(s). Tentacles can break off and remain on the skin, causing ongoing envenomation.
Stingrays cause intensely painful punctures or lacerations, often on a foot as the victim walks through shallow surf. Swelling and erythema are often present.
Other vertebrate fishes cause punctures with erythema, papules, burning, and itching. Vesicles, bullae, and/or ischemia may occur.
Sea urchins cause painful puncture wounds. Spines may break off into the wound, but dark dye deposited in the skin from the spines can mimic foreign bodies.
Generalized systemic symptoms (malaise, nausea, and headache) can occur after any envenomation.
Critically ill divers or swimmers pulled from the sea may have suffered a massive envenomation (look for lesions) or anaphylactic reaction to a venom. Deaths are more common in Australia and Asia.
Laboratory studies are not helpful.
Radiographs are indicated if foreign body (generally sea urchin, stingray, or fish spines) is suspected.
Be aware of venomous marine creatures in the area you practice, as well as their envenomation syndromes.
Consider envenomation in all cases of marine diving accidents, near-drownings, and in any swimmer or diver with painful or pruritic eruptions and/or puncture wounds.
Order radiographs if foreign bodies (spines) are suspected.
Treat envenomations by vertebrate fish (stingrays, lionfish, etc.) and sea urchins with analgesics and hot water immersion to inactivate the heat-labile venom. B
Stingray envenomations may cause pain for one or more weeks, but rarely require prophylactic antibiotics or admission. B
Although effective treatment seems to vary from one species to another, hot water (45°C) immersion appears to effectively treat pain after some jellyfish envenomations. B

Classic recommendations for invertebrate marine envenomations (jellyfish, man-of-war, anemone, etc.) involve inactivating nematocysts with acetic acid solution, scraping nematocysts from the area, and flushing copiously with sea water. C
Some envenomations require specific antivenom. These include species native to Australia and Asia such as the Australian box jellyfish, stonefish, and sea snakes. C
Use opiate analgesics and NSAIDs for pain control.
Use antipruritics such as diphenhydramine to control pruritus.
Commercial preparations such as Stingose and Sting-Aid (aluminum sulfate) have not been proved effective.
Topical anesthetics (e.g., lidocaine) can be applied, but their use has not been well-studied.
Corticosteroids may be used for recurrent dermatitis, although their efficacy has not been proved.
Antivenom is available for stonefish, Australian box jellyfish, and sea snake envenomations.
Administer tetanus prophylaxis.
The literature does not support the use of prophylactic antibiotics. Treatment of secondary bacterial infections should be directed at skin flora and Vibrio sp.
Treat anaphylactic reactions in the usual fashion.
Promptly remove foreign bodies (spines) resulting from stingray, fish, or sea urchin envenomations.
Despite classic teaching (see below), hot water (45°C) immersion appears to effectively treat pain after some jellyfish stings.

Without strong supportive evidence, classic teaching for invertebrate (e.g., jellyfish) stings is to inactivate stinging cells with 5% acetic acid solution (vinegar) or isopropyl alcohol, and then to remove the cells by scraping the skin or flushing copiously with seawater.
Other recommended agents (urine, olive oil, and papain) have been not proved effective. Applying liquor or rubbing affected areas may worsen symptoms.

A Cochrane review evaluating interventions to alleviate signs and symptoms from jellyfish stings found insufficient evidence for heat versus cold application as well as for multiple topical applications, based on very low certainty evidence.
For vertebrate fish and sea urchin envenomations, hot water immersion relieves the pain caused by the (heat-labile) venom.
Severe envenomations caused by deadly species may require ACLS protocol, including mechanical ventilation.
Pressure immobilization techniques (e.g., Sutherland wrap) and ice pack therapy have not been shown to be effective.
Admit patients if antivenom administration is necessary, for intractable pain, or for any severe envenomation.
Treat recurrent dermatitis with topical or systemic corticosteroids.
Bacterial infections may require antibiotics. Ulcers and skin necrosis can complicate wound healing. Recurrent dermatitis can occur.
Foreign bodies from stingrays, urchins, and fish spines can cause morbidity.
Persistent dermatitis, skin hyperpigmentation, lichenification, arthralgias, erythema nodosum, and delayed reactions to marine venoms are known to occur.
Most envenomations cause no more than an uncomfortable dermatitis or local pain, but recurrent dermatitis can occur. Full recovery within 1 to 2 weeks is typical with proper treatment. C
Rarely, envenomations can be life-threatening due to venom effects or anaphylaxis. C

Rapid deaths are reported after envenomation by box jellyfish, sea snakes, stonefish, blue-ringed octopus, and cone snails. Death can also occur as a result of massive exposure to tentacles, drowning, mechanical trauma from spines, or severe allergic reactions. C
Envenomations tend to be more severe in the very old and the very young, as well as those with a serious underlying illness.
